title: Sowing spinach
subtitle: A spring and autumn sowing crop that bolts in summer heat
excerpt: Spinach is a cool-season crop sown in March to May and again in August to September in the UK. It bolts quickly in long warm days. Two short sowings a year from a cool position give better results than trying to maintain a summer stand.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), salads section. RHS spinach growing guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA agricultural extension service, spinach production notes, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Spinach produces a central flower stem when days are long (above 14 hours) and temperatures are high. Once the stem appears the leaves become small, bitter, and fibrous. Spring sowings made after mid-May are likely to bolt by June. Autumn sowings made in August or September run through to November without bolting.

content.text: Spinach is a cool-season crop that runs to flower as days lengthen in summer. In the UK, March to early May and again in August to September are the productive sowing windows. Summer heat and long days cause it to
before the leaves are worth picking. Chard (Beta vulgaris var. cicla) is the summer substitute.

Spring window: March to early May. A March sowing gives picking from May; April and May sowings follow in June before bolting starts. Summer is not worth attempting except in cool northern gardens. Autumn window: late July (in the north) or August to mid-September. An August sowing gives leaves through October and into November. Under a cold frame or cloche, autumn-sown spinach can be harvested through December in mild winters.

Full sun in spring. Partial shade in late spring and summer extends the life of the crop before bolting. Moist, fertile, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.5 to 7.0. Spinach is shallow-rooted and dries out quickly; a soil with added compost suits it well. Add a general-purpose fertiliser before sowing if the soil is poor.

Sow 2.5 cm deep, seeds 2 to 3 cm apart, in rows 30 cm apart. Thin seedlings to 8 to 10 cm for a cut-and-come-again crop, or 15 cm for full-sized plants. Sow thinly: a dense stand bolts faster than a well-spaced one. Small, frequent sowings every three weeks are more productive than one large sowing.

Spinach germinates in five to fourteen days at 5 to 15°C. It germinates poorly above 20°C; summer sowings may fail in a warm seedbed. Soak the seed for a few hours before sowing to improve germination rate in warm conditions. Seedlings emerge as a pair of narrow oval leaves.

Water consistently; spinach needs steady moisture to slow bolting. A liquid feed every two weeks with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser encourages leaf growth. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep the plant producing. Once the central flower stem appears, the crop is over; compost the plant and resow.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: What goes wrong with spinach, and what to do.

items.symptom: Plants run to seed quickly after germination
items.cause: Sowing too late in the season (warm long days), or in a very sunny dry position.
items.fix: Sow by mid-May for spring crops. Move autumn sowings to a shaded north-facing position. Choose slow-bolting varieties such as Tornado or Perpetual Spinach.
Feed with a liquid nitrogen-rich fertiliser every two weeks. Add compost to the bed before the next sowing.
Cover with fine insect-proof mesh immediately after sowing. Flea beetle damage is cosmetic; a little makes little difference to yield.
